chunks: From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

There are two matters; whichever comes first causes the doubtful divorced woman to be considered divorced. She doubts her menstruation: if three white months pass through her without blood in them, she is divorced by them. And if three menstruations pass through her, with no three months between the two menstruations, she is divorced by the menstruation.

Ibn Abi Umayr said, Jamil said: The explanation of this is: if three months pass through her minus one day, then she menstruates, then three months pass through her minus one day, then she menstruates, then three months pass through her and she menstruates, then this woman considers herself bound by the menstruations in this manner and does not consider herself bound by the months. And if three white months pass through her and she does not menstruate in them, then she is divorced.

key_terms.الْمُسْتَرَابَةُ: The doubtful woman (regarding her waiting period)
key_terms.بَانَتْ: She is divorced / The bond is broken

ai.seo_question: How does a divorced woman determine her waiting period when she is unsure whether it is based on months or menstruation?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani's al-Istibsar clarifies the legal mechanism for resolving uncertainty in a divorced woman's waiting period (iddah) by prioritizing whichever condition—three months or three menstruations—is fulfilled first. It highlights the Shia juristic principle of 'sabaq' (precedence) in determining the finality of divorce, ensuring clarity in the transition from marital bond to independence. The detailed explanation by Ibn Abi Umayr underscores the precision required in distinguishing between continuous months and discrete menstrual cycles to avoid ambiguity in religious obligations.
